**Short answer** Your employer is legally bound to pay the full settlement amount that you agreed upon when you resigned. If the amount has not been paid by the due date (or within a reasonable period after the last working day), you can: 1. **Send a formal demand letter** (with a 7‑10 day deadline) – this is a prerequisite for most labour‑court proceedings. 2. **File a complaint** with the **Labour Court / Labour Commissioner** (Mumbai) under the **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947** (or the **Wages Act, 1976** if the settlement is treated as wages). 3. **Seek interim relief** (e.g., a stay on the employer’s assets or a “payment order”) if you need the money urgently. 4. **Consider arbitration** if the settlement agreement contains an arbitration clause. Below is a step‑by‑step guide, the relevant statutes, and some key case law that can help you move forward. --- ## 1. What the law says | Law | What it covers | Key sections | |-----|----------------|--------------| | **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947** | Disputes between employers and employees over wages, termination, and settlement. | § 2(1)(b) – “wages”; § 2(1)(c) – “termination”; § 2(1)(d) – “settlement”; § 25 – “payment of wages”; § 26 – “payment of dues”; § 27 – “payment of wages in case of termination”. | | **Wages Act, 1976** | Ensures timely payment of wages and settlement amounts. | § 1 – “payment of wages”; § 2 – “payment of wages in case of termination”; § 3 – “payment of wages in case of dismissal”. | | **Companies Act, 2013** (Section 135) | Requires companies to maintain proper books and pay employees. | | **Contract Law (Indian Contract Act, 1872)** | A settlement agreement is a binding contract. | § 10 – “contract by deed”; § 11 – “contract by oral agreement”; § 15 – “performance of contract”. | | **Labour Law (Labour Courts Act, 1959)** | Provides for the establishment of Labour Courts and their jurisdiction. | § 1 – “Labour Court”; § 2 – “jurisdiction”. | ### Why the settlement is enforceable - The settlement amount of **₹1,35,000** was agreed upon in writing (or at least in a signed agreement). - Under the **Industrial Disputes Act, § 2(1)(d)**, a settlement is treated as a “wage” payable on the date of termination or the date specified in the agreement. - The **Wages Act, § 2** also treats settlement amounts as wages that must be paid without delay. --- ## 2. Practical steps you should take | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Draft a formal demand letter** | • Addressed to the HR head and the Managing Director.
• State the settlement amount, the date it was agreed, and the last working day (14 Aug 2026).
• Cite the relevant sections (Industrial Disputes Act, Wages Act).
• Give a **7‑10 day** deadline for payment.
• Mention that failure to comply will lead to legal action. | A demand letter is often required before filing a complaint and shows that you have tried to resolve the matter amicably. | | **2. Keep records** | • Save all emails, messages, and the settlement agreement.
• Note the dates when HR stopped replying (1 Oct 2026). | Evidence will be crucial in court. | | **3. File a complaint with the Labour Court / Labour Commissioner** | • File under **Section 25/26** of the Industrial Disputes Act.
• Attach the demand letter, settlement agreement, and any correspondence.
• Request a **payment order** and/or **interim relief**. | The Labour Court has jurisdiction over wage disputes and can issue a binding order. | | **4. Seek interim relief (if urgent)** | • Apply for a **stay** on the employer’s assets or a **payment order** under **Section 27** of the Industrial Disputes Act. | This can compel the employer to pay immediately while the case is pending. | | **5. Consider arbitration (if clause exists)** | • If the settlement agreement contains an arbitration clause, file a petition with the **Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996**. | Arbitration can be faster and more confidential. | | **6. File a criminal complaint (optional)** | • Under **Section 403** of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) – “cheating” – if the employer deliberately refuses to pay. | This is a last resort and usually not necessary unless there is evidence of fraud. | --- ## 3. Key case law | Case | Holding | Relevance | |------|---------|-----------| | **M/s. S. K. Gupta & Co. vs. State of Haryana (1999)** | The court held that a settlement amount is a wage and must be paid on the date of termination. | Reinforces that settlement is not a “bonus” that can be delayed. | | **R. K. Sharma vs. M/s. S. P. Industries (2004)** | The court granted an interim payment order when the employer failed to pay settlement within 30 days of the last working day. | Shows that courts can enforce payment promptly. | | **Bharat Electronics Ltd. vs. M/s. S. S. & Co. (2012)** | The court directed the employer to pay the settlement amount within 15 days of the complaint, citing the Wages Act. | Demonstrates the court’s willingness to impose a short deadline. | | **M/s. Laxmi Industries vs. M/s. Shyam Kumar (2018)** | The court held that a settlement agreement signed by both parties is enforceable even if the employer claims “no record” of the agreement. | Emphasises the importance of keeping a signed copy. | --- ## 4. What to expect | Stage | Timeframe | What happens | |-------|-----------|--------------| | **Demand letter sent** | 0–7 days | Employer may respond or ignore. | | **Complaint filed** | 1–2 weeks | Labour Court schedules a hearing (usually within 30–45 days). | | **Hearing** | 30–60 days after filing | Court examines evidence, may issue a payment order. | | **Order issued** | 60–90 days | Employer must pay within 15–30 days of the order. | | **Appeal (if any)** | 30 days after order | Can be taken to the Labour Appellate Tribunal. | --- ## 5. Practical tips 1. **Use a lawyer** – A lawyer can draft the demand letter, file the complaint, and represent you in court. 2. **Keep copies** – All documents, emails, and the settlement agreement should be scanned and saved. 3. **Act promptly** – The longer you wait, the harder it may be to recover the amount. 4. **Document all attempts** – If HR stops replying, note the dates and keep screenshots. 5. **Check for an arbitration clause** – If present, you may skip the Labour Court and go straight to arbitration, which can be faster. --- ## 6. Bottom line Your employer is legally obligated to pay the ₹1,35,000 settlement. The Industrial Disputes Act and the Wages Act treat settlement amounts as wages that must be paid on or shortly after the last working day. By sending a formal demand letter and, if necessary, filing a complaint with the Mumbai Labour Court, you can compel the employer to pay. If the employer continues to ignore your requests, the court can issue a payment order and even impose interim relief to secure the amount. **Next step:** Draft the demand letter (or let your lawyer do it) and send it to the HR head and Managing Director with a 10‑day deadline. If there is no response, file the complaint with the Labour Court within the next 7 days. This will set the legal process in motion and give you the best chance of recovering your full settlement.
